items.title: Arithmetic Mean — ungrouped, grouped, combined & weighted
items.body:
## Formulae

| Case | Formula |
|---|---|
| Ungrouped | x̄ = (x₁ + x₂ + … + xₙ)/n |
| Grouped | x̄ = Σfx/Σf  (x = class mid-value) |
| Combined | x̄ = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂) |
| Weighted | x̄ = Σwx/Σw |

## Worked example (grouped)

Classes 0–10…40–50 with f = 5, 8, 15, 16, 6; mid-values 5, 15, 25, 35, 45.
Σfx = 25+120+375+560+270 = 1350, Σf = 50 ⇒ **mean = 1350/50 = 27**.

## Shortcuts & traps

- **Correcting a wrong value:** corrected mean = old mean + (Σcorrect − Σwrong)/n. (Work with the total Sum = mean × count.)
- **Adding/removing items:** find the new/removed sum as (new total − old total).
- **Change of origin/scale:** if y = a·x + b then ȳ = a·x̄ + b — mean shifts by b and scales by a.
- **Trap:** the combined mean is a *weighted* average, not the simple average of the two group means.
keyPoints: Ungrouped mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations.
Grouped mean = Σfx/Σf where x is each class mid-value.
Combined mean = (n₁x̄₁ + n₂x̄₂)/(n₁ + n₂) — weighted by group sizes.
Weighted mean = Σwx/Σw; equals the simple mean when all weights are equal.
Corrected mean = old mean + (Σcorrect − Σwrong)/n.
Under y = a·x + b the mean becomes a·x̄ + b (change of origin and scale).
items.mnemonic: Mean = 'total ÷ count' — always convert a mean back to a Sum (mean × count) before adding, removing or correcting values.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Mean

items.title: Median — ungrouped and grouped
items.body:
## Ungrouped (arrange in ascending order first)

- **Odd n:** Median = [(n+1)/2]ᵗʰ term.
- **Even n:** Median = average of the (n/2)ᵗʰ and (n/2+1)ᵗʰ terms.

## Grouped

Median = **L + [(N/2 − C)/f] × h**, where
L = lower limit of median class, N = Σf, C = cumulative frequency *before* the median class, f = frequency of the median class, h = class width. The median class is the one whose cumulative frequency first reaches N/2.

## Worked example (grouped)

f = 4, 5, 7, 10, 12, 8 (classes 0–10…50–60); N = 46, N/2 = 23. Cumulative 4, 9, 16, 26 ⇒ median class 30–40. Median = 30 + [(23 − 16)/10]×10 = **37**.

## Traps

- Forgetting to sort ungrouped data before picking the middle term.
- Using C = cf of the median class itself instead of the class *before* it.
- The median is a positional average, so it is **robust to outliers**.
keyPoints: Always sort data ascending before finding an ungrouped median.
Odd n: median = [(n+1)/2]ᵗʰ term; even n: mean of the two middle terms.
Grouped median = L + [(N/2 − C)/f] × h.
Median class = first class whose cumulative frequency ≥ N/2.
C is the cumulative frequency of the class BEFORE the median class.
The median is unaffected by extreme outliers (positional measure).
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Median

items.title: Mode & the empirical relation
items.body:
## Ungrouped

Mode = the value that occurs most frequently. A set may be unimodal, bimodal, or have **no mode** (all frequencies equal).

## Grouped

Mode = **l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h**, where
l = lower limit of the modal class, f₁ = frequency of the modal class, f₀ = frequency of the class before it, f₂ = frequency of the class after it, h = class width. The modal class is the one with the **highest frequency**.

### Worked example

Pets 1–2…5–6 with f = 5, 9, 3, 2, 1 ⇒ modal class 2–3 (l=2, f₁=9, f₀=5, f₂=3, h=1). Mode = 2 + (4/10) = **2.4**.

## Empirical relation (moderately skewed data)

**Mode = 3·Median − 2·Mean.** Equivalently, Mean − Mode = 3(Mean − Median). Use it when any one of the three is unknown.
keyPoints: Mode (ungrouped) = the most frequently occurring value; can be none, one or many.
Grouped mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h.
Modal class = the class with the highest frequency.
Empirical relation: Mode = 3·Median − 2·Mean (moderately skewed data).
The mode is the only measure usable for qualitative/categorical data.
items.mnemonic: Empirical order on a skewed curve: Mean pulled toward the tail, then Median, then Mode — 'Mode = 3 Median − 2 Mean'.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Mode

items.title: Dispersion basics — range & mean deviation
items.body:
## Range

- **Range = Highest − Lowest.** Simple but ignores all intermediate values.
- **Coefficient of range = (H − L)/(H + L)** — a unitless *relative* measure of spread.

## Mean deviation (MD)

**MD = (1/n)·Σ|x − A|**, where A is a chosen average (mean, median or mode) and |·| ignores signs. MD is **least when taken about the median**.

### Worked example (about the mean)

Data 6, 7, 10, 12, 13, 4, 8, 12 ⇒ mean = 9. Absolute deviations 3, 2, 1, 3, 4, 5, 1, 3 sum to 22 ⇒ **MD = 22/8 = 2.75**.

## Traps

- Range gives no information about the distribution of the middle values.
- In MD you must take **absolute** deviations, else the signed deviations about the mean sum to zero.
keyPoints: Range = Highest value − Lowest value.
Coefficient of range = (H − L)/(H + L) — unitless relative dispersion.
Mean deviation = (1/n)·Σ|x − A| using absolute deviations.
Mean deviation is minimum when measured about the median.
Signed deviations about the mean always sum to zero — hence use absolute values.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Range and Class Interval / Mean Deviation

items.title: Variance, standard deviation & choosing a measure
items.body:
## Variance & standard deviation

- **Variance σ² = (1/n)·Σ(x − x̄)²** — the mean of squared deviations.
- **Standard deviation σ = √variance** — same units as the data; the most-used spread measure.

### Worked example

Data 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 ⇒ mean 6. Squared deviations 16, 4, 0, 4, 16 sum to 40 ⇒ variance = 40/5 = **8**, SD = √8 ≈ **2.83**.

### Change of origin & scale

Under y = a·x + b: **variance ×a², SD ×|a|; adding b has no effect.** SD is unaffected by a shift of origin.

## Which measure to use?

| Situation | Best measure |
|---|---|
| Symmetric data, no outliers | Mean |
| Outliers / open-ended classes / skew | Median |
| Qualitative / most-frequent category | Mode |
| Overall spread about the mean | Standard deviation |
keyPoints: Variance σ² = (1/n)·Σ(x − x̄)²; standard deviation σ = √variance.
SD is in the same units as the data and is the most widely used dispersion measure.
Change of scale: variance ×a², SD ×|a|; change of origin (adding b) leaves both unchanged.
Use the mean for symmetric data, the median for skewed/outlier data, the mode for categorical data.
For the data 2,4,6,8,10 the population variance is 8 and SD ≈ 2.83.
items.source: local APPSC Quantitative Reasoning PDF — Variance and Standard Deviation

items.title: Moving averages & time-series trend
items.body:
A **moving average** smooths a time series so its underlying **trend** stands out, by replacing each block of consecutive values with their mean and sliding the block along one step at a time.

## Method (k-year moving average)

1. Average the first k values.
2. Drop the oldest value, add the next one, average again.
3. Repeat to the end. With n data points you get **(n − k + 1)** moving averages.

## Worked example (3-year)

Sales 30, 35, 25, 42, 62 →
- (30+35+25)/3 = 30
- (35+25+42)/3 = 34
- (25+42+62)/3 = 43

Trend values: **30, 34, 43** (rising).

## Notes & traps

- For an **odd** k the moving average is centred on the middle year; for an **even** k a second centring step is needed.
- A series in AP gives moving averages equal to each window's middle term.
- Moving averages reduce short-term fluctuation but **shorten** the series by (k − 1) terms.
keyPoints: k-year moving average = mean of each sliding block of k consecutive values.
Number of moving averages = n − k + 1.
Odd k centres on the middle year; even k needs an extra centring.
Moving averages smooth fluctuations to expose the trend, losing (k−1) terms.
items.mnemonic: Slide-and-average: drop the oldest, add the newest, re-mean.
items.source: standard APPSC/SSC statistics — moving averages / time series
